newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi puts his fate on line over Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi puts his fate on line over Albania.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi put his survival on the line on Wednesday in a desperate gambit to win parliamentary support for deployment of an Italian-led security force to Albania and save his unsteady government.

Grappling with the worst crisis of his office, he told the lower Chamber of Deputies he would ask President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to decide his fate if key ally Communist Refoundation deserted him in a vote on the mission later on Wednesday.
Scalfaro, the supreme arbiter in Italian politics, could in such an event either ask Prodi to tender his resignation or send him back to parliament for a confidence vote on the government.
Prodi's undertaking was wrested from him by the centre-right opposition as the price for voting with the government on a joint motion opening the way for the Albanian mission.

But it failed to move Refoundation, whose opposition to the Albania force has raised deep doubts about Prodi's ability to press on with a legislative programme full of tough economic decisions certain to raise more howls from the hard-left party.
"On Albania we will vote 'no,' as we have already stated," party chairman Armando Cossutta said.

He added, however, that the party would support Prodi in any subsequent confidence test as long as it was not on Albania. "We are against the Albania expedition but we are not against the government," Cossutta said.
Refoundation regards the proposed Albanian force as a neo-colonialist venture, one which co-incides with the 58th anniversary this week of the occupation of Albania by pre-war Fascist Italy.
Prodi, in office since May, cannot command a majority in the lower house without Refoundation, whose 34 deputies hold the balance of power. The vote was expected at around 1800 GMT.
Deployment of the multinational force, the first to be led by Italy, appeared not to be in danger since the centre-right Freedom Alliance also supports it.

But the opposition has exacted a high toll from Prodi for its backing, sensing it can embarrass him by insisting that he must acknowledge in parliament that his majority had been cut to shreds by the Refoundation mutiny.

Prodi took steps to meet the demand in his speech, noting that a Refoundation 'no' vote in the Senate (upper house) on Tuesday, when the government's own majority was enough to get its motion through, had shown his majority had problems.
"These problems...will become even clearer if, as possible, the Communist Refoundation group were also to vote against the government's recommendations in this house," Prodi said.

"For this reason...I declare now that if the dissent expressed by the Communist Refoundation group persists, I will go immediately to the head of state to inform him officially of the situation and await his evalution," Prodi said.
His statement was welcomed by Freedom Alliance leaders.

"Having always said that we needed to deploy the mission but also needed to certify the division in the (governing) majority, I personally feel more than satisfied," hard right leader Gianfranco Fini told reporters.

The rift over Albania has raised serious doubts in Prodi's coalition about the future of the difficult partnership with Refoundation. The main coalition parties now want a thorough review of the alliance to determine whether it can survive.

The Marxist-inspired party is at odds with the government on key economic issues, including a drive to cut social spending in order to put Italy in line to join Europe's planned single currency. Those issues are next on the agenda after Albania.
